title: Header JSON parse sampling and worker affinity experiment
content:
Summary:
This note captures a discrete investigation into short tail latency spikes observed during small payload requests (avg 5–50 bytes of JSON headers). Hypothesis: per-request JSON header validation and small-object allocation in Python are causing disproportionate CPU overhead and GIL contention in our default worker pool. The doc records sampling data, experiment permutations, microbenchmarks, and recommended mitigations for follow-up.

Context and motivation:
- Incident: transient 95th/99th percentile latency regressions on the hosted API for small requests after the routing change (see JIRA INF-7421). These spikes correlate with traffic bursts where request bodies are tiny but headers contain diagnostic JSON metadata (tracing, auth metadata).
- Existing observations: flamegraphs suggest lots of small C-Python frame time in json.loads, PyDict creation, and frame overhead for validation code paths. Tokenization investigations (prior) focused on model text tokenizers; this work focuses on HTTP layer JSON parsing and per-request lightweight validation.

Initial sampling method:
- Environment: dev cluster replica (c2-standard-like), single machine serving runtime; workload replay from golden trace (traffic-minutes sample).
- Tools: async-sampling profiler (py-spy), Linux perf for kernel/syscall view, flamegraphs (FlameGraph), tracemalloc snapshots for allocation hotspots.
- Sampling cadence: 1ms wall-clock, 60s traces during steady-state, also shorter 10s bursts to capture cold-start behavior.
- Metric of interest: CPU time in user-space attributed to parse/validation, average GIL hold time per request, number of PyObject allocations per request, context-switches/sec for worker threads.

Key microbenchmarks (local reproducer):
- baseline_python_json: Python json.loads on header string (avg size 230 bytes) repeated in a tight loop.
- orjson: same workload using orjson.loads.
- simdjson (pysimdjson): binding-based parse of the same string.
- validation_func: post-parse validation (small schema checks using plain if/for, vs pydantic v2 model parse).

Benchmark results (median of 10 runs, single core):
- baseline_python_json: 940 us / op
- orjson.loads: 190 us / op
- pysimdjson: 130 us / op
- validation_func (hand-rolled checks): 60 us additional
- pydantic v2 parsing + validation: 420 us additional

Observations:
- The Python stdlib json is extremely expensive for many tiny per-request parses — an order of magnitude slower than orjson/simdjson.
- The validation layer, even when small, adds measurable CPU; pydantic v2 is convenient but has large per-parse overhead.
- py-spy flamegraphs show significant time in _json.c (parsing) and PyDict_SetItem / object allocation frames.
- perf shows many futex waits when the worker pool is saturated and CPU migration happens across cores. Context switch rate increases during spikes.

Worker affinity experiment (two axes):
1) CPU isolation: run serving workers pinned to a contiguous set of cores using taskset + isolated CPUs (kernel boot param isolcpus) and configure the process to avoid scheduler migrations.
2) interpreter isolation: start groups of worker processes each with a dedicated core set (worker group A for parsing-heavy routes, group B for compute-heavy model traffic).

Results:
- Pinning workers reduced tail latency variability: 99th percentile dropped ~20% in controlled tests.
- Isolation reduced cross-core cache-thrashing and lowered context-switch rates by ~30%.
- However, strict affinity increases unfairness under bursty loads (some cores saturate while others idle) — must pair with proper autoscaling/burst policies.

GIL and subinterpreter note:
- We experimented briefly with Python subinterpreters to reduce contention for non-GIL-bound workloads. In our sampling they reduced apparent GIL hold times for validation-heavy requests but added complexity in C-extension compatibility and memory overhead. Not recommended for short-term rollout.

Optimization permutations tested in the replay environment:
A) Replace stdlib json with orjson for header parsing + hand-rolled validation (fast path).
B) Offload heavy schema validation to a background thread-pool using a lock-free queue; accept request with header-tagging and do async validation (eventual reject/corrections).
C) Use a C-accelerated parser (pysimdjson) when available, fallback to orjson.
D) Introduce per-worker small object pool / reuse buffers to avoid repeated PyObject churn for tiny dicts (object pooling via native extension).
E) Pin worker groups to cores and expose a 'parse-critical' route tag that routes small-header traffic to parsing-optimized workers.

Tradeoffs observed:
- A (orjson) gives largest single-line improvement with low integration cost. Code changes minimal; orjson binary is stable in our environment.
- B (async validation) reduces tail latency at the cost of immediate correctness guarantees; suitable for telemetry headers but not for auth checks.
- C (pysimdjson) is fastest in raw parse on our strings but bindings instability observed on some Linux kernels used in customers' private deployments.
- D (object pooling) reduces allocation counts but requires careful native code; increased memory retention and complexity.
- E (routing to specialized workers) gives operational control but increases resource usage and scheduling complexity.

Recommended short-term action plan (low friction):
1) Adopt orjson for header parsing in the request pipeline for the fast-path code path. Add feature-flag to toggle per-deployment. (Owner: Rafael)
2) Replace pydantic parsing in the hot path with hand-rolled minimal checks (explicit field presence, small type checks) for headers; keep full schema parsing in less-latency-sensitive paths. (Owner: Sana)
3) Apply soft CPU pinning on canary pool (taskset) for 2–3 worker groups to validate affinity benefits under production load. (Owner: Maya)
4) Add sampling instrumentation to record parse library used, parse time, and whether validation deferred. Surface on per-route console dashboard. (Owner: Observability team)

Recommended medium-term actions (investigate/validate):
- Prototype pysimdjson fallback for on-prem images where ABI matches; create integration tests across kernel/glibc variants.
- Evaluate a native extension that implements a tiny object pool for header dicts to reduce PyObject churn.
- Revisit subinterpreter usage only if cross-extension compatibility issues can be solved and memory overhead controlled.

Instrumentation to add before rollout:
- Histogram buckets for parse latency (us), tagged by parser implementation (stdlib/orjson/simdjson).
- Trace span for validation step and indicator if validation was deferred.
- GIL hold-time sampling metric (aggregate) to detect other hotspots.

Open questions / risks:
- Are there secrets/auth headers that cannot be validated asynchronously? If yes, we must keep strict sync validation for those routes.
- Does orjson produce identical behavior wrt float parsing/decimal/strictness our clients depend on? Need matrix tests across clients.
- Pysimdjson ABI instability risk on older on-prem customer kernels — requires packaging strategy.

Appendix: small reproducer (python snippet)
- baseline reproducer (loop) using stdlib json vs orjson: included here to run quickly on dev box.

>>> import time, json
>>> import orjson
>>> s = '{"trace_id":"abcd1234","meta":{"env":"prod","ver":1}}'
>>> def std_parse():
...     for _ in range(10000):
...         json.loads(s)
...
>>> def or_parse():
...     for _ in range(10000):
...         orjson.loads(s)
...
>>> t0 = time.time(); std_parse(); print(time.time()-t0)
>>> t1 = time.time(); or_parse(); print(time.time()-t1)

Action items / next steps (short list):
- [ ] Prod canary: push orjson fast-path behind feature-flag on 10% of requests routing to canary pool. Collect parse metrics for 24h. (Rafael)
- [ ] Add manifest of headers that are safe for async validation vs those requiring sync checks. (Sana)
- [ ] Run affinity canary with pinned workers for a week, monitor tail latency and CPU efficiency. (Maya)
- [ ] Add e2e tests to catch semantic differences between stdlib json and orjson for edge cases observed in our client corpus. (QA)

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: pick the low-effort, high-impact change (orjson) for the first rollout. If that reduces tail significantly, follow with routing/affinity/async validation for further gains.
- Keep an eye on memory usage: orjson returns bytes -> native objects; ensure we aren't holding large temporary buffers longer than needed.

Related tickets and references:
- JIRA INF-7421: intermittent tail latency post-routing-change
- GH redwood/serving-runtime#1182: implement parser switchover flag
- Internal perf board: small-object allocation patterns (Q2 2025)

End of note.
